fields.title: Release notes are written for the user
fields.keyTakeaway: Release notes answer the question "what should I do differently now", not "what we built". A change that changes nothing for the reader does not belong in them.
fields.checkQuestion: "Refactoring the signing module, dependency updates." Who is this addressed to?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **which changes should be communicated to users?** Emphasis on "which": communicating everything is the same as communicating nothing.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer the question.** Release notes turn into a tracker dump. People stop reading them, and when a truly important change comes along, it goes unnoticed too.
fields.blocks/2/title: What makes it into release notes
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Changes what a person does** — included, first.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Removes what people complained about** — included, referencing how it was before.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Requires user action** — must be included and kept separate.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Changes nothing on the outside** — excluded, no matter how much work went into it.
fields.blocks/3/text:
From tracker: "Document list query optimized. Signing module refactoring. Dependencies updated. Mass selection added."

For user: "You can now sign multiple certificates at once: check the boxes and click “Sign”. Previously you had to open each one — this was the most requested feature."

One change out of four, but people will actually read it.
fields.blocks/3/title: Reestr, two versions of the same release notes
fields.blocks/4/text: Short release notes do not replace breaking change notifications: if a user must take action, communicate this separately and in advance, not as a line item in a general list.
